Pre Launch Mandate

Pre-launch mandate (Day 0 readiness gate)

1. What this is

The Pre-launch mandate defines:

👉 What must be completed before activating Day 0

Day 0 is not a date.
It is a decision backed by readiness.

This mandate ensures:

  • We do not start execution prematurely
  • We enter markets with clarity and structure
  • Core dependencies are already in motion

2. What good looks like

Before calling Day 0:

Market clarity

  • Market selected with clear rationale
  • Key cities/zones identified
  • Competitor landscape understood

On-ground understanding

  • Market visited by central team / GM
  • First-hand understanding of:
    • Demand
    • Supply ecosystem
    • Logistics feasibility
    • Competition

Hiring readiness

  • GM hired
  • Head of Commercial hired
  • Head of Real Estate hired
  • Head of Fulfilment hired

Initial execution alignment

  • Functions aligned on:
    • What needs to be done
    • Who owns what
  • No ambiguity in ownership

👉 Simple test:
 If Day 0 is triggered tomorrow, can the team start executing immediately?

3. Principle

  • Do not confuse intent with readiness
  • Do not start execution without ownership
  • Do not rely on assumptions — rely on on-ground validation
  • Day 0 should unlock execution, not create confusion

4. Execution (step-by-step)

Step 1: Decide the market

What you need to do:
  • Identify target country
  • Align internally on:
    • Strategic importance
    • Market potential

Step 2: Define initial market view

What you need to do:
  • Identify:
    • Key cities
    • Priority zones
  • Map:
    • Competitors
    • Demand clusters

Step 3: Conduct market visit

What you need to do:
  • Visit the market physically
  • Validate:
    • Customer behaviour
    • Store formats
    • Pricing levels
    • Delivery feasibility
    • Local trends

Step 4: Initiate hiring

What you need to do:
  • Start hiring for:
    • GM
    • Commercial head
    • Real estate head
    • Fulfilment head
  • Build candidate pipeline

Step 5: Align central team

What you need to do:
  • Ensure each function knows:
    • Their role in launch
    • Their responsibilities
  • Align on:
    • Execution expectations

Step 6: Validate readiness

Before calling Day 0, confirm:

  • Market understood
  • Team in place
  • Ownership clear

Step 7: Trigger Day 0

👉 Once all conditions are met:

  • Day 0 is activated
  • Timeline begins (Day 0 → Day 90)
  • Execution engine starts

5. Checklists (subtasks)

Task: Pre-launch readiness

Subtasks:
  • Market selected
  • Cities/zones identified
  • Competitor mapping done
  • Market visit completed
  • Insights documented
  • GM hired
  • Commercial head hired
  • Real estate head hired
  • Fulfilment head hired
  • Joining timelines confirmed
  • Functions aligned
  • Polygons drawn

6. Audit (pass / fail)

Audit: Day 0 readiness

PASS if:
  • All critical roles hired
  • Market validated on ground
  • Ownership clearly defined
FAIL if:
  • Hiring incomplete
  • No market visit
  • Lack of clarity on execution

👉 Failed audit = Do not start Day 0

7. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Calling Day 0 based on urgency
  • Starting without key hires
  • Skipping market visit
  • Assuming market dynamics
  • Lack of ownership clarity

8. Simple way to think about it

Day 0 should feel like:

👉 “We are ready to execute”

Not:

👉 “We will figure things out as we go”

Key takeaway

Day 0 is not the start of thinking.

It is the start of execution.

👉 If the foundation is weak, the entire launch slows down.

Introduction

Welcome to noon Minutes

noon Minutes is one of the core businesses at noon — bringing everything to every door, every single day, in 15 minutes.

The power of convenience and urgency creates something customers rely on for both their big and small needs.

The business works only if customers truly believe we are adding value to their daily lives.

From the outside, it looks simple:
A customer selects items on the app, and they arrive at their door in 15 minutes or less.

Behind the scenes, it is a tightly run system — designed to deliver a best-in-class experience while growing sustainably from day 1.

Where we are today

  • UAE: 150+ dark stores — clear number one in the market since launch in 2022
  • KSA: 100+ dark stores — number two in the market, with a clear path to number one by 2026 (achieved within two years of inception)

What makes the business work

Everything comes down to getting six things right:

  • Assortment — having the right products
  • Availability — ensuring they are always in stock
  • Speed — executing flawlessly when an order comes in
  • Execution — seamless cross-functional coordination to deliver within 15 minutes
  • Quality - delivering items at the standard that the customer expects
  • Pricing - providing affordability for customers

These are not just metrics.
They define how the business operates.

What this means for the team

The business reflects the team behind it.

To win, we operate with:

  • The right skill sets
  • High availability and responsiveness
  • Speed in execution
  • Strong ownership
  • Tight cross-functional collaboration

Your mandate

Your goal is simple:

Launch a new country, build a strong team, and dominate the market within 3 months.

For context, we are not entering empty markets.

We are entering markets where:

  • Competitors are already live
  • Supply is locked
  • Customers have habits
  • Pricing expectations are set

The bar is not to launch.
The bar is to dominate — fast.

What this playbook will do

This playbook is built to help you execute.

It includes:

  • Clear steps on what needs to be done
  • Checklists to ensure nothing is missed
  • Trackers to monitor progress
  • Practical guidance to drive execution

If followed well, this will enable you to launch and win a new market within 3 months.

Execution Timeline

Execution timeline (country launch)

Pre Day 0: Foundation (Pre-launch mandate)

Goal

Ensure readiness before execution begins

What needs to be done

Market
  • Market selected
  • Cities/zones identified
  • Competitor benchmarking initiated
On-ground validation
  • Market visit completed
  • Demand, supply, logistics feasibility understood
Hiring
  • GM hired
  • Head of Commercial hired
  • Head of Real Estate hired
  • Head of Fulfilment hired
Planning
  • AOP aligned
  • Store rollout plan defined
  • Cost assumptions understood

Output (Day 0 trigger)

  • Core team in place
  • Market understood
  • Execution ownership defined

👉 Day 0 begins

Day 0–30: Set the foundation

Goal

Lock supply, stores, pricing, and execution structure while building a world-class team

1. Commercial & assortment

  • Competitor mapping done
  • Core SKU list defined
  • Supplier onboarding initiated
  • Assortment gaps identified

2. Pricing & promos

  • Pricing logic applied (base pricing engine)
  • KVI list identified
  • Initial price benchmarking completed

3. Instock (availability setup)

  • Demand planning started
  • Inbound flows defined
  • Initial inventory model created

4. Dark stores (real estate + fit-outs)

  • Locations shortlisted and finalised
  • Lease agreements in progress
  • Fit-outs initiated (racks, cold rooms)

5. Logistics (speed readiness)

  • Rider hiring pipeline started
  • Delivery zones defined
  • SLA benchmarks set

6. Hiring (extended team)

  • Function teams hiring in progress
  • Ownership defined across functions

7. Systems & tracking

  • Task tracker live
  • AOP vs execution aligned
  • PnL tracking setup

Output by Day 30

  • Assortment defined
  • Suppliers in pipeline
  • Pricing baseline ready
  • Dark store pipeline active
  • Tracker live with ownership

Day 30–60: Build and go live

Goal

Launch first dark store and stabilise operations

1. Commercial & assortment

  • Core assortment live
  • Depth built in key categories
  • Missing SKUs continuously added

2. Pricing & promos

  • Competitive pricing live
  • Promos deployed for KVIs
  • Burn tracking started

3. Instock (availability execution)

  • Fill rates stabilised
  • Stock-outs actively resolved
  • Supply gaps fixed in real time

4. Dark stores

  • Fit-outs completed
  • Stores stocked and operational
  • Audit completed → PASS for launch

5. Logistics (15-min execution)

  • Riders onboarded
  • Delivery flows tested
  • SLA adherence ensured

6. Customer experience

  • Ordering → delivery flow stabilised
  • Early issues identified and fixed

Output by Day 60

  • First dark store live (~Day 50)
  • Orders flowing
  • SLAs and fill rates stabilising
  • Pricing competitive

Day 60–90: Scale and dominate

Goal

Expand coverage and become a top player

1. Commercial & assortment

  • Assortment exceeds competitors
  • Strong category depth
  • Vendor network expanded

2. Pricing & promos

  • Daily price gap tracking
  • Optimised promo strategy
  • Controlled burn with high impact

3. Instock

  • High fill rates across stores
  • Efficient replenishment
  • Reduced wastage

4. Dark store expansion

  • Additional stores launched
  • Coverage expanded
  • Density improved

5. Logistics

  • Rider utilisation optimised
  • Delivery times consistently within SLA
  • Coverage vs cost balanced

6. Growth & marketing

  • Traffic scaled
  • Conversion improved
  • Promo abuse controlled

7. PnL tracking

  • AOP vs actual tracked
  • Cost per order optimised
  • PC1 improving

Output by Day 90

  • ~90% geographic coverage
  • Strong operational stability
  • Competitive positioning achieved

👉 Target: Top player in the market

Execution is not linear.

Org Structure

Organisation structure

Understanding the organisation structure is critical to mobilising a market and reaching the desired OPD (orders per day) target.

The objective is not just to support the market until launch, but to support it until it reaches target OPD with a positive PnL.

The structure is designed to ensure:

  • Clear ownership across functions
  • Fast decision-making
  • Strong execution discipline
  • Continuous performance tracking

What the structure enables

The organisation structure is not just functional — it is the enabler of how we operate:

  • Ownership is default
     We don’t say “that’s not my job”
  • Speed over perfection
     We move fast and correct quickly
  • Dashboards > stories
     Data is the single source of truth
  • Standards are binary
     We either meet targets or we don’t
  • We improve constantly
     Every. Single. Day.

How to use the structure

The sub-tabs provide visibility into all the expert functions that support market launches, including:

  • Commercial
  • Fulfilment
  • Logistics
  • Instock
  • Finance
  • Growth
  • HR

Each function exists to enable you to reach the end goal: dominating the market.

Working with central functions

While each market behaves differently, a large part of success comes from:

  • Leveraging central expertise
  • Aligning early with functional owners
  • Using existing frameworks instead of rebuilding from scratch

Central teams bring:

  • Proven playbooks
  • Market learnings
  • Execution benchmarks
  • The Minutes culture

Your role is to adapt and apply, not reinvent.

Core team structure

You are required to build the following core team in-market:

Head of fulfilment

  • Owns warehouse and dark store operations
  • Ensures smooth inbounding and order processing

Head of logistics

  • Owns rider supply and delivery performance
  • Ensures SLA adherence and customer experience

Head of real estate

  • Owns dark store location identification and rollout
  • Works with central real estate on site finalisation

Head of facilities management

  • Owns store upkeep and operational readiness
  • Ensures stores are compliant and fully functional

Head of grocery commercial

  • Owns grocery assortment and vendor relationships
  • Ensures depth in high-frequency categories

Head of core commercial

  • Owns non-grocery categories
  • Drives assortment expansion beyond essentials

Head of in-stock

  • Owns SKU availability
  • Drives demand planning and replenishment

Head of growth & marketing

  • Owns traffic, conversion, and demand generation

How the team should operate

  • Work cross-functionally, not in silos

  • Move with speed and ownership

The strength of your team determines the speed of your launch and the quality of your scale.

Planning & Tracking

Planning & tracking (AOP to execution)

1. What this is

Planning and tracking ensures:

👉 There is clarity on where the business is going (AOP)
👉 There is visibility on where the business is today (Live PnL)

2. Planning = AOP (annual operating plan)

What AOP is

The Annual Operating Plan (AOP) is created by the Central Strategy Team.

It defines:

  • Market ambition
  • Growth targets
  • Investment required
  • Profitability journey

👉 This is the foundation of the business for that country

What AOP includes

Growth plan
  • Orders per day (OPD)
  • GMV / NMV growth
  • Dark store expansion

👉 Example from AOP:

  • Dark stores scaling from 6 → 45
  • OPD scaling to ~40K+
Revenue & contribution
  • Revenue
  • COGS
  • PC1 and PC1%

👉 Defines:

  • Unit economics
  • Contribution per order
Cost structure

Variable costs

  • Logistics cost
  • Fulfilment cost
  • Payment cost
  • Customer support

Fixed costs

  • Rent
  • Staff
  • Overheads
Investment plan

CAPEX

  • Dark store setup
  • Infrastructure

OPEX

  • Marketing
  • Operations
  • Central costs
Profitability journey
  • PC1 → PC2 → PC3 → EBITDA

👉 Shows:

  • Efficiency improvements over time
  • Reduction in losses
  • Path to profitability

3. What good looks like (planning)

  • Clear targets:
    • OPD
    • GMV
    • Dark stores
  • Clear cost understanding:
    • Cost per order
    • Fixed vs variable
  • Clear profitability path:
    • PC1 → PC4

👉 Simple test:
 Clarity exists on:

  • Scale
  • Cost
  • Profitability

4. Tracking = live PnL (execution reality)

What tracking is

Tracking is enabled through:

👉 Live PnL view from Finance

What it provides

Growth vs plan
  • Orders vs AOP
  • GMV vs AOP
  • Store rollout vs plan
Profitability vs plan
  • PC1
  • Cost per order
  • Burn
Cost control
  • Logistics efficiency
  • Fulfilment efficiency
  • Marketing spend

5. Planning vs tracking (simple view)

LayerWhat it answers
AOP (Planning)Where the business should be
Live PnL (Tracking)Where the business actually is

👉 The gap between the two = what needs to be fixed

6. How to use this framework

Step 1: Understand the AOP

Clarity required on:

  • Target OPD
  • Store rollout plan
  • Cost assumptions
  • Profitability milestones

Step 2: Track regularly

Monitor:

  • Orders vs plan
  • Cost vs plan
  • PC1 vs plan

Step 3: Identify gaps

Assess:

  • Growth vs target
  • Cost vs assumptions
  • Execution vs plan

Step 4: Take action

If gaps exist:

  • Growth gap → pricing, promos, assortment need adjustment
  • Cost gap → logistics, fulfilment need optimisation
  • Scale gap → store rollout needs acceleration

7. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: AOP understanding

  • Growth targets understood
  • Store rollout plan clear
  • Cost structure understood
  • Profitability path clear

Task: Tracking

  • Live PnL accessible
  • Metrics tracked regularly
  • Variance vs AOP identified

Task: Actioning

  • Gaps identified
  • Owners assigned
  • Fixes implemented

8. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • AOP clearly understood
  • Tracking is consistent
  • Gaps are actively addressed

FAIL if:

  • No visibility on targets
  • No tracking discipline
  • No action on gaps

9. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Treating AOP as static
  • Infrequent tracking
  • Ignoring cost metrics
  • Over-focusing on growth alone
  • Not linking actions to PnL

10. Simple way to think about it

👉 AOP is the plan
 👉 PnL is the truth

Key takeaway

The business is not run on intuition.

👉 It is run by continuously comparing:

Plan vs Reality → and fixing the gap

Registration

Legal entity registration

Setting up the legal entity is the first step to entering a new market.
Without this, nothing moves — from signing leases to onboarding vendors and processing payments.

The objective is to establish a compliant, fully functional entity that enables commercial and operational execution without delays.

What good looks like

  • Legal entity incorporated and compliant
  • All required licenses secured
  • Bank accounts operational
  • Ability to sign contracts (real estate, vendors, riders)
  • Payments and collections enabled

Core principles

Start early

Legal timelines are often the longest lead items — initiate immediately.

Parallelise wherever possible

Do not wait for one step to complete before starting the next.

No shortcuts on compliance

Delays later are costlier than doing it right upfront.

Enable business, don’t block it

The goal is to ensure smooth execution across all functions.

Key responsibilities

Entity setup

  • Finalise entity structure (legal form, ownership)
  • Register company with relevant authorities
  • Secure trade name and approvals

Licensing & compliance

  • Obtain required business licenses
  • Secure regulatory approvals (as per country requirements)
  • Ensure compliance with local laws (labour, tax, operations)

Banking & financial setup

  • Open corporate bank accounts
  • Enable payment processing (vendor payments, customer collections)
  • Align with finance on approvals and controls

Contracts & legal framework

  • Enable signing of:
    • Lease agreements (dark stores)
    • Vendor contracts
    • Rider / logistics agreements
    • Marketing and agency contracts
  • Work closely with legal to ensure contract readiness

How to operate

  • Engage legal from Day 0
  • Track all approvals and dependencies centrally
  • Identify critical blockers early (licenses, bank approvals, etc.)
  • Follow up aggressively on timelines

What to avoid

  • Delaying entity setup
  • Assuming timelines without validation
  • Starting operations without required approvals
  • Fragmented tracking of legal dependencies

Success indicators

  • Entity fully operational before key commercial activities
  • No delays in signing leases or onboarding vendors
  • Payments flowing smoothly
  • Full compliance with local regulations

Key mindset

Legal setup is not a backend activity.
It is a critical path item for launch readiness.

If done right:

  • Execution moves faster
  • Risks are minimised
  • Scale becomes easier

Dark Store

Dark Stores

Dark stores are the backbone of Noon Minutes.
They are where assortment, availability, and speed come together to deliver the 15-minute promise.

If the dark store is right — the business works.
If it is broken — nothing else matters.

Detailed Darkstores guidelines

Darkstore go live - checklist

What good looks like

  • Store designed for 2000+ OPD scalability
  • Assortment placed for fast picking and minimal errors
  • High fill rates and stock accuracy
  • Optimised pick path → pack → dispatch flow
  • Fully compliant, clean, and operationally disciplined

Core principles

Speed is designed — not achieved

15-minute delivery starts with store layout and processes.

Every second in picking matters

Bad placement = slow picking = broken promise.

Availability is everything

If it’s not in stock, it doesn’t exist.

Standardisation drives scale

Every store should follow the same playbook.

1. Store design and layout

Principle

Design stores for speed, scalability, and accuracy.

Execution

Store sizing

  • Target ~3000+ sqft for ~2000 OPD stores
  • Separate clearly:
    • Inbound staging
    • Storage (ambient, chiller, frozen)
    • Outbound & packing
    • Rider waiting area

Storage zoning

  • Ambient (largest share)
  • Chiller (0–4°C)
  • Frozen (-18°C to -23°C)

👉 Use cold rooms for high OPD stores (better capacity and efficiency)

Category placement

  • A+ / A (fast moving) → closest to outbound
  • B → mid distance
  • C → farthest

👉 Top 500 SKUs must be closest to packing

Pick path

  • Standard: Z → A flow (end near outbound)
  • Objective:
    • Minimise movement
    • Reduce picking time
    • Improve accuracy

2. Inventory and availability

Principle

Availability drives conversion.
Stock-outs kill trust.

Execution

Inventory management

  • Daily tracking of stock levels
  • Real-time visibility of stock-outs
  • Immediate action on supply gaps

Category strategy

  • Focus:
    • High-demand SKUs first
    • Depth in key categories
  • Balance:
    • Breadth vs velocity

Non-happy flows (critical discipline)

Separate and manage:

  • Expiry
  • Damage
  • RTV
  • Returns

👉 Never mix with live inventory

3. Inbound to outbound operations

Principle

Seamless flow = speed + accuracy.

Execution

Inbound

  • Receive → inspect → record
  • Fast putaway into correct zones

Putaway

  • Place SKUs in designated locations
  • Maintain structured binning system

Picking & packing

  • Follow defined pick path
  • Batch intelligently
  • Minimise picker movement

Outbound

  • Fast packing at designated stations
  • Smooth rider handoff

Returns flow

  • Inspect → classify → restock or dispose

4. Assets and infrastructure

Principle

Right assets = efficient operations.

Execution

Core assets

  • Storage racks (ambient, chiller, freezer)
  • Suprabins + dividers
  • Packaging stations
  • Pigeon holes (sorting)
  • PDAs for picking

Consumables

Maintain buffers:

  • Packaging bags
  • Labels & stickers
  • Tapes & seals
  • Admin supplies

👉 Track daily. Reorder before depletion.

5. Manpower and productivity

Principle

Right manpower = stable operations.

Execution

Staffing model

  • Inbound team
  • Outbound (pickers)
  • Inventory team
  • Supervisors

Planning approach

  • Based on OPD forecast
  • Adjust using productivity benchmarks
  • Ensure minimum staffing threshold

Focus metrics

  • Items picked per picker
  • Orders processed per hour
  • Store throughput

6. Systems and tech setup

Principle

No system → no scale.

Execution

Core systems

  • Warehouse database setup
  • WMS configuration
  • Location mapping

Customer side

  • Store mapped on app
  • Delivery zones defined
  • Pricing and catalogue integrated

Optimisation

  • Pick path configuration
  • Barcode mapping
  • Inventory sync

7. Facilities and maintenance

Principle

Operational stability requires maintenance discipline.

Execution

Critical maintenance

  • Chillers and freezers
  • Air conditioning
  • Plumbing

Pest control

  • Mandatory twice a month
  • Zero tolerance for issues

Breakdowns

  • Log immediately
  • Follow SLA-based resolution
  • Escalate if delayed

8. 5S and operational discipline

Principle

Clean, organised stores run faster.

Execution

5S framework

  • Sort → remove clutter
  • Set in order → structured placement
  • Shine → clean daily
  • Standardise → uniform processes
  • Sustain → continuous discipline

Key rules

  • No clutter
  • No blocked aisles
  • No products on floor
  • Clear zone demarcations

9. Real estate and compliance

Principle

Location quality drives delivery performance.

Execution

Site selection

  • Strong demand zones
  • Good access for riders
  • Parking availability

Pre-launch approvals

  • Trade license
  • Lease agreements
  • Local compliance

Operational readiness

  • Layout approved
  • Facilities functional
  • Store codes generated

10. Launch readiness checklist

Before go-live

  • Store layout completed
  • Inventory stocked
  • Systems live
  • Team trained
  • Riders available
  • SLAs tested

After go-live

  • Monitor operations daily
  • Fix gaps immediately
  • Stabilise fill rates and speed
  • Improve continuously

Key takeaway

Dark stores are not warehouses.
They are high-speed retail engines.

Winning requires:

  • Precision in design
  • Discipline in execution
  • Relentless daily improvement

DS - Real Estate

Finding and closing locations

Principle

Pick locations that help you deliver in 15 minutes consistently and operate efficiently at scale.

What you need to do

Scouting

Start with the market — not the property.

Identify the right zones first:

  • High population density
  • Strong demand pockets (residential + offices)
  • Areas where competitors are already active
  • Gaps in competitor coverage (white spaces)

How to approach:

  • Break the city into delivery clusters (zones)
  • Aim for complete coverage, not random store placement
  • Map competitors and their dark store locations

Rule:
 Don’t fall in love with a property.
First lock the zone → then find the property.

Shortlisting options

For each zone:

  • Identify multiple options (minimum 2–3 per zone)
  • Track all options in a sheet (rent, size, pros/cons)

Never depend on a single site — deals fall through often.

Evaluating a site

Before finalising, physically inspect and validate:

Access & operations
  • Can riders enter/exit easily?
  • Is there parking or waiting space?
  • Is the road accessible during peak hours?
Logistics feasibility
  • Is there space for loading/unloading?
  • Can trucks reach the location easily?
  • Any restrictions on delivery timings?
Store suitability
  • Is the size sufficient for:
    • Storage
    • Packing
    • Rider movement
  • Can you fit:
    • Racks
    • Cold rooms
    • Packing stations
Building constraints
  • Any restrictions on:
    • Commercial activity
    • Noise / operations
    • Working hours
  • Is landlord/building management supportive?
Delivery coverage check
  • Does the location allow good 15-minute coverage radius?
  • Does it overlap efficiently with other planned stores?

Negotiation

Your goal is not just to get a store —
it is to get a commercially viable store.

Rent
  • Benchmark against nearby properties
  • Avoid overpaying for “premium” locations without ROI
Payment structure

Push for:

  • Rent-free period (for fit-out time)
  • Lower upfront deposits
  • Flexible payment schedules
Terms to protect
  • Clear exit clause (in case store underperforms)
  • Reasonable lock-in period
  • Clarity on:
    • Maintenance costs
    • Utility responsibilities
Mindset
  • Be firm but practical
  • Speed matters — don’t lose good sites due to over-negotiation

Closure

Once agreed:

  • Finalise terms (LOI if applicable)
  • Work with legal to draft and review agreements
  • Coordinate with finance for payments

Approvals

Ensure:

  • Trade license compatibility
  • Building approvals (if required)
  • No regulatory blockers

Output

By the end of this stage, you should have:

  • Locations finalised for each zone
  • Lease agreements signed
  • Commercial terms locked
  • Sites ready to move into fit-out

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Picking a cheap but operationally poor location
  • Not checking rider access properly
  • Finalising without multiple backup options
  • Ignoring exit clauses
  • Delaying decisions and losing good sites

Simple way to think about it

A good location should answer:

  • Can we deliver fast from here?
  • Can we operate smoothly from here?
  • Does this make financial sense?

If the answer is not clearly yes → don’t take the site.

DS - Fitout & Racking

Fit-outs (dark stores)

Fit-outs convert an empty site into an operational dark store.

This is where delays usually happen.
Your job is to ensure the store is built fast, correctly, and ready for operations without rework.

Please do find the checklist in the end that is to be followed for ensuring that a dark store is launched ready.

Principle

Build the store for:

  • Speed (fast picking and dispatch)
  • Flow (no bottlenecks)
  • Scalability (can handle higher OPD later)

1. What needs to be set up

There are three parts to fit-outs:

  • Civil and infrastructure work
  • Racking and storage setup
  • Equipment and operational readiness

2. Critical items (must be ready before go-live)

These are non-negotiable.
Do not go live if any of these are incomplete.

A. Civil and basic infrastructure

  • Flooring completed and usable
  • Electrical setup (power points, lighting)
  • Backup power (if required)
  • Internet connectivity

B. Storage setup (racking)

  • Ambient racks installed
  • Chiller units installed (0–4°C)
  • Freezer units installed (-18°C) or cold rooms
  • Proper zoning:
    • Ambient
    • Chiller
    • Frozen

C. Layout and flow

  • Clear inbound area (for receiving stock)
  • Defined storage zones
  • Packing stations ready
  • Clear pick path (no obstructions)
  • Rider handover area

D. Equipment

  • Packing tables
  • Pigeon holes / sorting bins
  • Suprabins and dividers
  • PDAs / scanning devices

E. Safety and compliance

  • Fire safety (extinguishers, exits)
  • CCTV installed and working
  • Basic safety checks completed

F. Operational readiness

  • Store cleaned and organised
  • No clutter or blocked aisles
  • All zones clearly marked

Output (critical readiness)

  • Store can:
    • Receive inventory
    • Pick and pack orders
    • Dispatch riders smoothly

3. Non-critical items (can improve post go-live)

These should be done, but should not delay launch.

A. Optimisation items

  • Additional racks for expansion
  • Improved storage density
  • Layout fine-tuning

B. Aesthetic improvements

  • Branding inside the store
  • Signage improvements
  • Non-essential visual elements

C. Process enhancements

  • Better bin labelling
  • Improved zoning refinements
  • Advanced pick path optimisation

D. Additional assets

  • Extra equipment buffers
  • Additional packing stations (if not needed immediately)

4. How to manage fit-outs

Planning

  • Lock layout before starting work
  • Align with:
    • Fulfilment
    • Facilities
    • Procurement

Execution

  • Track progress daily
  • Follow up aggressively with vendors
  • Do not wait for issues to escalate

Coordination

  • Ensure dependencies are aligned:
    • Power before equipment
    • Racks before stocking
    • Internet before systems

Pre-launch check

  • Walk the store physically
  • Simulate:
    • Picking
    • Packing
    • Rider movement

👉 If anything feels slow → fix it before launch

5. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Starting fit-out without final layout
  • Poor rack placement → slow picking
  • Not testing rider movement
  • Delays due to vendor misalignment
  • Launching with incomplete critical items

6. Simple way to think about it

Before go-live, ask:

  • Can we pick fast?
  • Can we pack smoothly?
  • Can riders move without friction?

If not → fix before launching

Key takeaway

Fit-outs are not about building a store.
They are about building a high-speed execution engine.

If done right:

  • Launch is smooth
  • Operations stabilise faster
  • Scaling becomes easier

2. Procurement & Replenishment Protocol
  • Inventory Tracking: Store Leads must conduct a daily/weekly physical count of packaging and labeling materials.
  • Reorder Points: Procurement should be triggered when stock reaches buffers to account for lead times.

DS- Payments

After negotiation: closing the deal (operations)

Once commercial terms are agreed, your job is to convert the deal into a signed agreement and enable payments without delays.

Step 1: Get the draft agreement

  • Request the first draft of the rent agreement from the property dealer / landlord
  • Do a quick check to ensure:
    • Commercial terms match what was agreed
    • No obvious mismatches

Step 2: Share with legal for review

What the legal team does

  • Reviews the agreement language
  • Ensures terms are:
    • Mutual and fair
    • Not one-sided
    • In line with company standards
  • Flags:
    • Risky clauses
    • Missing protections
    • Required changes

How to share with legal

  • Reach out to procurement
  • Upload the draft on SpotDraft
  • Tag the relevant stakeholders:
    • Legal
    • Finance

Step 3: Review and iteration

  • Legal and finance review the draft
  • If required:
    • Senior management approvals are taken
  • Comments are consolidated

Back-and-forth with landlord

  • Share revised draft with:
    • Legal / business / finance comments
  • Landlord reviews and responds
  • Update the draft based on discussions

👉 This process may repeat multiple times — follow up actively

Step 4: Finalisation and signing

Once all parties align:

  • Final version is uploaded on SpotDraft
  • Agreement is:
    • Signed by the landlord
    • Counter-signed by Noon

👉 At this stage, the contract is legally executed

Step 5: Vendor creation and payments

If advance rent / deposit is required:

What you need to do

  • Create landlord as a vendor on the MSA Dashboard
  • Upload:
    • Signed agreement (SpotDraft copy)
  • Raise payment request (Create a service PO)
  • Incase you are stuck, please reach out to finance.

    ***Exact Process for making sure payments are processed

Finance role

  • Verifies documents
  • Processes approvals
  • Releases payment

Step 6: Completion

Once:

  • Agreement is signed
  • Payments are processed

👉 The site is fully secured and ready for fit-out

Output

  • Signed rent agreement (SpotDraft completed)
  • Landlord onboarded as vendor
  • Payments processed
  • Store ready to move into build phase

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Not checking draft vs agreed commercial terms
  • Delays in uploading to SpotDraft
  • Not following up on legal comments
  • Missing vendor creation → delaying payments
  • Starting fit-out without signed agreement

Simple way to think about it

Negotiation is not done until:

  • The contract is signed
  • Payments are cleared
  • Site is secured

Commercial

Commercial & assortment

Commercial and assortment are the foundation of the business.

They determine:

  • What the customer sees
  • What the customer buys
  • Whether the business makes money

If this is weak, nothing else scales.

What good looks like

  • Equal or better assortment vs top competitors
  • Strong depth in high-frequency categories
  • Competitive pricing on key SKUs
  • High availability (minimal stock-outs)
  • Positive contribution margin over time

Core principles

Assortment wins demand

If the customer searches, we should have it.

Price builds habit

Customers should not feel we are more expensive.

Availability builds trust

If we don’t have it when needed, we lose the customer.

Commercial closes outcomes

Tracking is not enough — gaps must be closed.

Key responsibilities

Assortment

  • Benchmark competitor assortment at category and SKU level
  • Identify top-selling and high-frequency SKUs
  • Build core assortment first, not long-tail
  • Ensure depth in key categories (not just breadth)
  • Continuously plug assortment gaps

Vendor onboarding

  • Onboard vendors with the right commercial terms
  • Negotiate rebates, margins, and supply commitments
  • Prioritise reliable suppliers over fragmented supply
  • Lock key brands early

Pricing

  • Track competitor pricing at SKU level
  • Maintain price parity or better in the first phase
  • Identify and monitor KVIs (known value items)
  • Deploy targeted discounts where required
  • Avoid blanket discounting that impacts contribution

How to operate day-to-day

  • Review assortment gaps vs competition regularly
  • Track pricing gaps daily
  • Convince vendors to get heavy deals, create IPs with growth to add orders
  • Work closely with:
    • In-stock (availability)
    • Pricing (competitiveness)
    • Growth (demand signals)
  • Focus on closing issues, not just reporting them

What to avoid

  • Building large but irrelevant assortment
  • Ignoring price perception on key items
  • Scaling with low availability
  • Over-reliance on discounts to drive demand

Success indicators

  • Customers consistently find what they need
  • Prices feel competitive
  • Fill rates remain high
  • Repeat behaviour improves
  • Contribution margins stabilise

Key mindset

Commercial is not a support function.
It is the engine of the business.

If done right:

  • Demand builds
  • Trust builds
  • Margins follow

Execution

Commercial (execution through burn list)

📎 Burn List:

Your job:
👉 Move every task to closure
👉 Ensure what goes live is complete, competitive, and reliable

What good looks like (commercial)

At launch, commercial is working well if:

Assortment

  • We have equal or better assortment vs top competitor
  • All high-demand SKUs are present
  • Key categories have depth (not just surface coverage)
  • No obvious gaps when comparing with competitors

Vendors

  • All priority vendors are:
    • Onboarded
    • Contracted
    • Ready to supply
  • Clear POC exists for every vendor
  • Vendors are responsive and aligned on timelines

Pricing

  • We are:
    • At par or better on KVIs
    • Not visibly more expensive
  • Discounts are:
    • Targeted
    • Strategic
    • Not random

Availability

  • High fill rate on:
    • Core SKUs
    • Top categories
  • No repeated stock-outs on:
    • High demand items

Data & systems

  • All SKUs are:
    • Created
    • Uploaded
    • Error-free
  • Costs are:
    • Accurate
    • Complete
    • Usable for pricing & PnL

Launch readiness

  • Inventory is:
    • Inbound planned
    • Delivered on time
  • Pricing and deals are:
    • Live before launch
  • End-to-end flow works:
    • Listing → ordering → fulfillment

👉 Simple test:
 If a customer opens the app, they should feel:
“I get everything I need, at the right price, and it’s available.”

Principle

Commercial = closing gaps

If it is not:

  • Onboarded
  • Uploaded
  • Priced
  • Stocked

👉 It is not done

How the commercial work flows

(Your existing structured phases remain unchanged below 👇 — this now sits on top of it as the quality bar)

How to use this with the burn list

For every task in the burn list, ask:

  • Does this move us closer to:
    • Better assortment?
    • Better pricing?
    • Better availability?

If not → deprioritise
If yes → close it fast

What bad looks like (so you avoid it)

  • SKUs live but not relevant
  • Vendors onboarded but not supplying
  • Prices uploaded but uncompetitive
  • Inventory planned but not delivered
  • Data uploaded but incorrect

👉 This leads to:

  • Low conversion
  • Poor retention
  • Broken launch

Key takeaway

The burn list tells you what to do
 This section tells you what good looks like

👉 Your job is not to finish tasks
👉 Your job is to launch a winning assortment

Content

Content (SKU information & imaging)

1. What this function is responsible for

Content is responsible for:

  • Ensuring every SKU has complete, accurate, and high-quality information
  • Making products:
    • Discoverable
    • Understandable
    • Trustworthy

Content includes:

  • Product title
  • Attributes (size, brand, category, etc.)
  • Images
  • Taxonomy
  • Volumetrics
  • Shelf life & storage

2. Why content matters

1. Conversion

Customers cannot touch or inspect products.

👉 Content replaces the physical experience.

  • Clear title → faster decision
  • Good images → higher trust
  • Complete details → fewer drop-offs

2. Discoverability

  • Search and filters depend on:
    • Correct taxonomy
    • Accurate attributes

👉 Poor content = product is invisible

3. Operational accuracy

  • Logistics depends on:
    • Volumetrics
  • Instock depends on:
    • Correct SKU mapping

👉 Bad content breaks operations

4. Speed of scaling

  • High SKU volumes → require:
    • Structured templates
    • Clean workflows

👉 Poor content = rework + delays

👉 Simple test:
 Can a customer understand and trust the product in <5 seconds?

3. What good looks like (100% coverage)

Coverage

  • 100% SKUs have:
    • Title
    • Attributes
    • Images
    • Taxonomy
    • Cost
    • Barcode

Accuracy

  • No:
    • Wrong brands
    • Incorrect sizes
    • Duplicate SKUs

Image quality

  • Resolution: 800 × 1100
  • Aspect ratio: 3:4
  • White background
  • Correct product

System readiness

  • SKU successfully created (ZSKU generated)
  • No upload errors
  • All attributes validated

👉 Simple test:
 SKU is searchable, visible, accurate, and ready to sell

4. Content creation flow (end-to-end)

Step 1: Vendor data collection

  • Vendor submits product details via template
  • Data includes:
    • Product name
    • Brand
    • Size
    • GTIN/barcode

👉 Incomplete data = delays

Step 2: Data validation

Validate:

  • Category (taxonomy)
  • Title format
  • Mandatory attributes
  • Dropdown values

👉 Common issues:

  • Invalid brands
  • Missing attributes
  • Incorrect formats

Step 3: SKU creation (ZSKU)

  • Upload via:
    • Commercial Toolkit / Seller Lab
  • System generates:
    • ZSKU (unique identifier)

👉 Errors must be corrected and re-uploaded

Step 4: Content upload (attributes)

Using Commercial Toolkit:

  • Upload SKU content template (SCT)
  • Fill:
    • Mandatory fields
    • Product attributes

👉 Toolkit acts as:

  • Central system for SKU creation & updates

Step 5: Image upload

Option 1: Manual upload
  • Upload images directly to SKU
  • Reflects in ~15 minutes
Option 2: Bulk upload

Tools:

  • Mario
  • MobaXterm
Process:
  • Rename images using GTIN/NIN
  • Maintain:
    • Correct format
    • Folder structure
  • Generate CSV
  • Upload via toolkit

👉 Bulk upload improves speed significantly

Step 6: Additional attributes

Upload:

  • Taxonomy
  • Volumetrics
  • Shelf life
  • Storage conditions

👉 Done via:

  • Minutes toolkit / importers

Step 7: Cost & barcode mapping

Barcode mapping
  • Manual (Seller Lab) OR
  • Auto (Minutes toolkit)
Cost upload
  • Initial cost (importer)
  • Cost list via RO tool

👉 Required for:

  • Pricing
  • PnL visibility

Step 8: SKU goes live

Once all steps are complete:

  • SKU becomes:
    • Visible
    • Searchable
    • Orderable

5. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: SKU creation

  • Vendor data received
  • Data validated
  • SKU created (ZSKU)

Task: Content upload

  • Attributes filled
  • Template uploaded
  • Errors resolved

Task: Image upload

  • Images prepared (format correct)
  • Images uploaded
  • Correct product displayed

Task: Go-live readiness

  • Taxonomy set
  • Volumetrics uploaded
  • Cost uploaded
  • Barcode mapped

6. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • 100% SKUs have full content
  • Images meet standards
  • No validation errors
  • SKUs visible and searchable

FAIL if:

  • Missing attributes
  • Incorrect images
  • SKU errors
  • Incomplete uploads

7. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Uploading incomplete templates
  • Ignoring validation errors
  • Wrong or low-quality images
  • Duplicate SKU creation
  • Missing barcode/cost mapping

8. Simple way to think about it

Content is done when:

👉 The SKU is:

  • Correct
  • Complete
  • Customer-ready

Key takeaway

Content is not a backend task.

👉 It directly drives:

  • Conversion
  • Trust
  • Scale

Rebates and Margins

Margins & rebates (commercial fundamentals)

1. What this function is responsible for

Margins and rebates are responsible for:

  • Defining how much is earned per SKU
  • Ensuring sustainable unit economics
  • Structuring vendor partnerships
  • Supporting pricing and promotions

This is the foundation of profitability at SKU level.

2. What good looks like

Commercial strength

  • Strong margins negotiated with vendors
  • Rebates structured to improve profitability

Sustainability

  • SKUs contribute positively (PC1)
  • No dependence on excessive discounting

Clarity

  • Clear understanding of:
    • Cost price
    • Selling price
    • Margin
    • Rebates

👉 Simple test:
 After pricing and promos, does the SKU still make money?

3. How to think about margins

1. Margin is not just markup

Margin is:

Selling Price – Cost Price

But in reality, it must cover:

  • Logistics cost
  • Fulfilment cost
  • Payment cost
  • Discounts (burn)

👉 True margin = what is left after all costs (PC1)

2. Not all SKUs behave the same

KVIs (Known Value Items)
  • Low margin
  • High visibility

👉 Role:

  • Drive traffic
  • Stay competitive
Core SKUs
  • Moderate margin

👉 Role:

  • Balance growth and profitability
Long tail
  • Higher margin

👉 Role:

  • Generate profit

3. Margin is designed, not accidental

Margins come from:

  • Vendor negotiation
  • Product selection
  • Pricing strategy

👉 Weak margins at sourcing = weak business later

4. What are rebates

Definition

Rebates are:

👉 Additional earnings received from vendors
👉 Over and above base margin

Types of rebates

1. Back margin
  • % rebate on purchases
  • Improves effective margin
2. Volume rebates
  • Linked to:
    • Purchase quantity
    • Sales targets
3. Promotional support
  • Vendor-funded discounts
  • Reduces promo burn
4. Listing / placement support
  • Paid by vendors for:
    • Visibility
    • Campaigns

5. How margins and rebates work together

Base margin

  • Comes from cost vs selling price

Rebates

  • Improve effective margin

👉 Final profitability =

Base Margin + Rebates – Costs – Discounts

6. Execution (step-by-step)

Step 1: Vendor onboarding

  • Negotiate:
    • Cost price
    • Margin
    • Rebates

Step 2: Define commercial terms

Ensure clarity on:

  • Base margin %
  • Rebate structure
  • Payment terms

Step 3: Align with pricing

  • Ensure:
    • Pricing remains competitive
    • Margins are protected

Step 4: Support promos

  • Use:
    • Vendor-funded discounts
  • Reduce:
    • Internal burn

Step 5: Track performance

Monitor:

  • Margin per SKU
  • Rebate realisation
  • PC1 impact

7. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: Vendor setup

  • Cost price agreed
  • Margin negotiated
  • Rebates defined

Task: Commercial validation

  • Margin supports PC1
  • Pricing feasible
  • No negative contribution

Task: Execution

  • Costs uploaded
  • Rebates tracked
  • Pricing aligned

8. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • Margins sufficient to cover costs
  • Rebates clearly defined and realised
  • SKUs contribute positively

FAIL if:

  • Margins too low
  • No rebate support
  • Negative contribution SKUs

9. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Focusing only on selling price
  • Ignoring backend rebates
  • Weak vendor negotiation
  • Over-reliance on discounts
  • Not tracking realised margins

10. Simple way to think about it

Margins and rebates answer:

👉 “Are we making money on what we sell?”

Key takeaway

Revenue drives growth.
Margins drive survival.

👉 Without strong margins and rebates, scale only increases losses.

SOP for Rebates Upload

Comp benchmarking

Product mapping (competition benchmarking execution)

1. What this is

The Product Mapping Tool is used to:

  • Map competitor SKUs → Noon SKUs
  • Measure:
    • Price Index
    • Assortment Gaps
  • Enable:
    • Pricing decisions
    • Commercial actions

2. What good looks like (based on this tool)

Coverage

  • ≥90% SKUs mapped in key categories
  • High mapping depth on:
    • Top SKUs
    • High demand categories

Accuracy

  • Correct SKU-to-SKU matches
  • No:
    • Wrong brand matches
    • Size mismatches
    • Variant mismatches

Visibility (what your screen should tell you)

From your UI:

  • “Mapped products” should keep increasing
  • “To be mapped” should continuously decrease
  • Partial mappings should be actively resolved

👉 Simple test:
 If you open this dashboard, can you immediately see:

  • What’s mapped
  • What’s missing
  • Where to act

3. How to use this screen (practical)

Top bar filters (control layer)

  • SKU search → find specific items
  • Category filter → focus on priority categories
  • Brand filter → focus on key brands
  • Status filter:
    • Unmapped → highest priority
    • Partial → next priority
    • Mapped → validation

Mapping buckets (important)

Unmapped

👉 Highest priority

  • These are assortment gaps OR missing mappings

Partial

👉 Medium priority

  • SKU exists but:
    • Not fully matched across competitors
  • Needs:
    • Completion

Mapped

👉 Validation stage

  • Ensure:
    • Accuracy
    • No wrong matches

SKU row (what to look at)

Each row gives:

  • SKU
  • Product title
  • Brand
  • Category
  • Price
  • Mapping %

Mapping column (critical)

Example:

  • 3/6 mapped (50%)

👉 Means:

  • 3 competitors mapped
  • 3 missing

4. Execution (how to operate daily)

Step 1: Start with unmapped

  • Filter → “Unmapped”
  • Map:
    • High priority SKUs first
    • High demand categories

Step 2: Move to partial

  • Complete missing mappings
  • Ensure:
    • All major competitors covered

Step 3: Validate mapped

  • Check:
    • Brand match
    • Size match
    • Variant match

Step 4: Prioritisation logic

Always prioritise:

  • KVIs (price sensitive items)
  • High frequency SKUs
  • Core categories

5. AI mapping (how to use properly)

What the tool does

  • Suggests top 5 matches
  • Shows similarity score

When to trust it

  • Similarity > 90%
  • Clear visual + title match
  • Price range reasonable

When to override

  • Wrong variant (e.g. 1L vs 500ml)
  • Different SKU pack
  • Wrong brand

👉 Rule:
 AI helps speed. Humans ensure accuracy.

6. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: SKU mapping

  • Unmapped SKUs identified
  • High priority SKUs mapped
  • Partial mappings completed
  • AI suggestions reviewed
  • Incorrect mappings corrected

Task: Validation

  • KVIs verified
  • High-volume SKUs validated
  • No major mismatches

7. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • ≥90% mapping in key categories
  • High accuracy on KVIs
  • No obvious mismatches

FAIL if:

  • Large unmapped pool
  • Incorrect matches
  • Missing high-demand SKUs

8. What this feeds into (important)

This tool directly powers:

Pricing

  • Price Index
  • Price gap identification

Commercial

  • Assortment gaps
  • Vendor onboarding

Growth

  • Promo strategy
  • KVI positioning

9. What to improve (based on your roadmap)

You already mentioned:

  • Serviceability mapping → 🔥 very powerful
  • Price trends → critical
  • Better automation

Add this thinking:

👉 Add “Impact tagging”

  • Mark SKUs as:
    • KVI
    • High demand
    • Long tail

So teams focus on what matters.

10. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Mapping everything equally (no prioritisation)
  • Blindly trusting AI
  • Ignoring partial mappings
  • Not revisiting mapped SKUs

11. Simple way to think about it

This tool answers:

👉 “Are we competitive?”

Through:

  • What we sell
  • What we’re missing
  • How we’re priced

Key takeaway

Mapping is not a data task.

👉 It is the foundation of pricing + assortment strategy

Pricing & Promos

Pricing (how we think and act)

1. What pricing is responsible for

Pricing decides:

  • What the customer sees on the app
  • How competitive we are in the market
  • How much we earn per order (PC1)

It sits at the intersection of:

  • Competition
  • Customer behaviour
  • Profitability

2. What good looks like

Customer view

  • Prices feel:
    • Competitive
    • Fair
  • No obvious reason to switch to a competitor

Business view

  • We maintain:
    • Positive contribution (PC1)
  • No uncontrolled discounting

Execution view

  • Prices are:
    • Consistent
    • System-driven
    • Not manually random

👉 Simple test:
 Are we competitive where it matters, and profitable where it doesn’t?

3. How to think about pricing

1. Not all SKUs matter equally

There are 3 buckets:

KVIs (Known Value Items)
  • High visibility
  • Frequently compared

👉 Must be:

  • At par or cheaper than competitors
Core SKUs
  • Regularly purchased
  • Moderate visibility

👉 Must be:

  • Competitive
  • Not necessarily cheapest
Long tail
  • Low visibility
  • Rarely compared

👉 Can be:

  • Priced for margin

2. Competition defines the ceiling

  • Customers compare across apps
  • If we are clearly expensive → we lose

👉 So:

  • Benchmark constantly
  • React quickly

3. Profitability defines the floor

  • We cannot price below:
    • Sustainable PC1

👉 Even when discounting:

  • Know the cost
  • Control the burn

4. Pricing is layered

Pricing is not one number.

It has 3 layers:

Base price (pricing engine)
  • System-defined
  • Based on:
    • Competition
    • Cost
    • PC1
Promotional price
  • Temporary
  • Used to:
    • Close gaps
    • Drive growth
Effective price (customer sees)
  • Final price after:
    • Discounts
    • Campaigns

4. How pricing decisions are made

Step 1: Check competitor pricing

  • Identify:
    • Primary competitor in the market
    • Secondary competitors

👉 If competitor price exists:

  • Stay:
    • At par or slightly lower

Step 2: Check thresholds

  • Ensure:
    • Pricing does not break PC1 limits

👉 If competitor price is too low:

  • Do not blindly match
  • Cap at acceptable level

Step 3: Use fallback logic (if no competitor)

When no competitor price exists:

  • Use MSRP (if available)
  • Use cost-based pricing (PC1 logic)
  • Use standard markup (last fallback)

Step 4: Apply promos (if needed)

If base price is not competitive:

  • Use promos to:
    • Close gaps
    • Drive conversion

👉 But:

  • Always control burn

5. What you need to track daily

Competitiveness

  • Price Index vs competitors
  • KVI pricing gaps

Profitability

  • PC1
  • Burn

Execution

  • Incorrect pricing
  • Missing promos

6. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Pricing everything the same
  • Over-discounting without tracking burn
  • Ignoring competitor pricing
  • Not prioritising KVIs
  • Manual overrides without logic

7. Simple way to think about it

Pricing is a balance:

👉 Be competitive where customers look
👉 Be profitable where they don’t

Key takeaway

Pricing is not about being cheapest.

👉 It is about being smartly competitive and sustainably profitable

Promos

Promotions (pricing execution layer)

1. What this function is responsible for

Promotions are responsible for:

  • Making SKUs competitive in the market
  • Driving conversion and demand
  • Closing pricing gaps vs competitors
  • Controlling discount burn (cost of promotions)

Promos are how we act on pricing decisions.

2. What good looks like

Competitiveness

  • KVIs are:
    • At par or better vs competitors
  • No visible pricing disadvantage

Control

  • Burn is:
    • Tracked
    • Within limits
  • No uncontrolled discounting

Execution

  • Promos:
    • Go live on time
    • Apply to correct SKUs
    • Reflect correctly on the app

👉 Simple test:
 Are we competitive where needed, without overspending?

3. Principle

  • Promos are a precision tool, not blanket discounting
  • Always know:
    • Why the promo exists
    • How long it runs
    • How much it costs
  • Focus on:
    • High-impact SKUs (KVIs, high demand)
  • Control burn at all times

4. How to think about promos

When to use promos

Use promos to:

  • Close pricing gaps vs competitors
  • Boost conversion on key SKUs
  • Support launch or campaigns

When NOT to use promos

  • To fix bad pricing decisions
  • Without understanding burn
  • On low-impact SKUs

5. How promos work (simple)

Core structure

  • A promo can have:
    • Multiple SKUs
  • A SKU can:
    • Be part of multiple promos
  • Only:
    • One promo is active per SKU per warehouse

👉 Latest updated promo takes priority

Burn logic

Two levels:

Global burn
  • Total limit for the promo
  • Once reached → promo stops
SKU burn
  • Limit per SKU
  • Once reached → SKU stops using promo

👉 Always define burn limits

6. Execution (step-by-step)

Step 1: Define promo objective

  • What are we solving?
    • Price gap
    • Conversion
    • Campaign

Step 2: Identify SKUs

  • Prioritise:
    • KVIs
    • High demand SKUs

Step 3: Set pricing

  • Define:
    • Promo price
    • Burn per unit

Step 4: Create promo

  • Create promo code
  • Define:
    • Country
    • Scope (all stores or specific stores)

Step 5: Upload SKUs

  • Upload:
    • SKU list
    • Prices
    • Dates
    • Burn limits

Step 6: Validate

  • Ensure:
    • Correct SKUs
    • Correct prices
    • PC1 checks pass

Step 7: Go live

  • Confirm:
    • Pricing visible on app
    • SKUs active

Step 8: Monitor

  • Track:
    • Burn
    • Performance
  • Adjust or stop if needed

7. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: Promo setup

  • Objective defined
  • SKUs selected
  • Prices decided
  • Burn limits defined

Task: Upload

  • Promo code created
  • Scope defined
  • SKUs uploaded
  • Dates correct

Task: Validation

  • PC1 checks passed
  • SKUs live correctly
  • Prices visible

Task: Monitoring

  • Burn tracked
  • No overspend
  • Promo performing as expected

8. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • Promos applied correctly
  • Pricing visible on app
  • Burn within limits
  • No SKU errors

FAIL if:

  • Incorrect pricing
  • SKUs not live
  • Burn exceeded unexpectedly
  • Wrong SKUs selected

9. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Discounting everything equally
  • Ignoring burn tracking
  • Uploading incorrect SKUs
  • Not validating before go-live
  • Running promos without clear objective

10. Simple way to think about it

Promos are done right when:

👉 We win on price where it matters
👉 We control cost while doing it

11. Resources

📎 Sample promo upload file

👉 PCC 5 - promos

🎥 Promo upload walkthrough video

👉Pricing crash course 5 - promos - 2024/11/18 15:00 GMT+04:00 - Recording

Key takeaway

Promos are not about giving discounts.

👉 They are about buying growth efficiently and intentionally
