Checklist - commercial

Assortment readiness (pre go-live checklist)

1. What this is

Assortment readiness ensures:

👉 The right SKUs are created, uploaded, and ready to sell
 👉 All legal, commercial, and system dependencies are completed

This is the final gate before inventory flows and pricing goes live

2. What good looks like

Completeness

  • All required SKUs:
    • Created
    • Uploaded
    • Visible in system

Commercial readiness

  • Vendors:
    • Fully onboarded
    • Contracts signed
    • Rebates defined

System readiness

  • SKUs:
    • Have content
    • Have cost
    • Are ready for pricing & ordering

👉 Simple test:
 Can a PO be raised and fulfilled without any blockers?

3. Principle

  • Assortment is not ready until:
    • It is sellable
    • Not just identified
  • Dependencies must be:
    • Completed end-to-end
    • Not partially

4. Execution (step-by-step)

Step 1: Legal entity (LE creation)

What needs to be done

  • Create Legal Entity via tool
  • Get approvals completed

Why it matters

  • Required for:
    • Vendor onboarding
    • Contracts
    • Payments

Output

  • Legal entity created and approved

Step 2: MPA creation (vendor commercial setup)

What needs to be done

  • Create MPA (Master Purchase Agreement)
  • Add:
    • Finance emails
    • GRN emails
    • RO emails
  • Upload:
    • Legal documents (BDA)
  • Add:
    • Fixed rebate lines

Why it matters

  • Enables:
    • Purchasing
    • Rebate tracking
    • Vendor payments

Output

  • MPA live with all required details

Step 3: Contract execution (SpotDraft)

What needs to be done

  • Draft contract via SpotDraft
  • Get:
    • Internal approvals
    • Vendor approval
  • Finalise:
    • Signed agreement

Why it matters

  • Legal protection
  • Commercial clarity

Output

  • Contract executed and signed

Step 4: SKU creation

What needs to be done

  • Build Master SKU List (MSL)
  • Create SKUs in system

Inputs required

  • Vendor catalogue
  • Category mapping
  • Attributes

Why it matters

  • SKUs are the base unit of the business

Output

  • SKUs created (ZSKUs generated)

Step 5: SKU uploads (content + system readiness)

What needs to be done

  • Upload:
    • Attributes
    • Taxonomy
    • Images
    • Costs
  • Follow:
    • Commercial upload SOP

Why it matters

  • Makes SKUs:
    • Visible
    • Searchable
    • Sellable

Output

  • SKUs fully uploaded and system-ready

5. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: Legal & commercial setup

  • LE created and approved
  • MPA created and approved
  • Rebate lines added
  • Contracts signed via SpotDraft

Task: SKU readiness

  • MSL created
  • SKUs created
  • Content uploaded
  • Images uploaded

Task: System readiness

  • Costs uploaded
  • Taxonomy set
  • SKUs visible in system

6. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • All SKUs created and uploaded
  • Vendors fully onboarded
  • Contracts signed
  • Costs and rebates defined

FAIL if:

  • Missing SKUs
  • Incomplete uploads
  • Contracts not signed
  • Costs/rebates missing

7. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Creating SKUs without full content
  • Missing rebate setup in MPA
  • Delayed contract execution
  • Partial uploads
  • Not validating SKU readiness

8. Simple way to think about it

Assortment is ready when:

👉 SKUs exist
👉 Vendors are onboarded
👉 Contracts are signed
👉 System is ready to sell

Key takeaway

Assortment readiness is not just about listing products.

👉 It is about ensuring everything required to sell those products is complete

Logistics

Logistics (launch readiness view)

What good looks like (at launch)

P0: Delivery zones defined (non-negotiable)

This is the first and most critical step.

What needs to be done

  • Define delivery zones per dark store
  • Ensure:
    • 15-minute feasibility
    • Sufficient order density

What to consider

  • Distance from store
  • Traffic conditions
  • Population density
  • Expected demand pockets

Why this is critical

  • Defines:
    • SLA feasibility
    • Rider requirement
    • Cost per order

👉 If zones are wrong:

  • Riders cannot meet SLA
  • Costs increase
  • Customer experience breaks

👉 Output

  • Finalised delivery zones mapped per store

1. Rider supply aligned to zones

  • Riders planned based on:
    • Zone size
    • Expected demand
  • Buffer available for:
    • Peak hours

2. Rider vendors closed

  • Vendors:
    • Identified
    • Negotiated
    • Contracted
  • Clear agreements on:
    • Cost per delivery
    • SLA
    • Availability

3. Rider onboarding complete

  • Riders:
    • Hired
    • Trained
  • Ready for:
    • Day 1 operations

4. SLA is achievable

  • 15-minute delivery validated across zones

Includes:

  • Picking
  • Handover
  • Travel

5. Store → rider handoff optimised

  • Picking time controlled
  • Riders do not wait excessively
  • Orders move quickly to dispatch

6. Order flow tested

  • Pilot orders completed
  • End-to-end flow validated

7. Monitoring in place

  • Ability to track:
    • Delivery time
    • Rider availability
    • Delays

8. Utilisation aligned to OPD (critical)

  • Each dark store has:
    • Target OPD
  • Rider count aligned to:
    • Peak demand

Balance required

  • Overstaffed →
    • High cost
  • Understaffed →
    • SLA failure

👉 Goal:
 Optimal riders per store based on OPD and zone design

Simple way to think about it

Everything starts with zones:

👉 Zones → define riders → define SLA → define cost

Key takeaway

Logistics is not ready when riders are hired.

👉 It is ready when:

  • Zones are correct (P0)
  • Riders are aligned to zones
  • SLA is achievable
  • Utilisation is efficient

Logistics execution & metrics

Logistics (Last Mile Execution & Metrics)

1. What this function is responsible for

Logistics ensures:

  • Orders are delivered within 15 minutes
  • Rider supply matches demand
  • Delivery is fast, reliable, and efficient

This function directly drives:

👉 Customer experience
👉 SLA adherence
👉 Cost per order
👉 Scale (OPD readiness)

2. Core idea

Logistics = Time optimisation + Rider utilisation

Every order is a race against time, broken into measurable components.

3. Delivery flow (time breakdown)

Each order is tracked across 4 stages:

1. Pick Up Time

Order placed → Rider picks order from store

  • Depends on:
    • Picking speed (Operations)
    • Rider availability

👉 Goal: Minimise waiting time at store

2. Last Mile Time

Pickup → Rider reaches customer location

  • Depends on:
    • Delivery radius
    • Routing
    • Traffic

👉 Goal: Optimised delivery routes

3. Handover Time

Arrival → Customer receives order

  • Depends on:
    • Customer readiness
    • Rider efficiency

👉 Goal: Quick, smooth handoff

4. Return Time

Post-delivery → Rider ready for next order

  • Depends on:
    • Routing back
    • Dispatch system

👉 Goal: Fast turnaround

4. Core metrics to track

A. SLA Metrics (Customer-facing)

1. 95th Percentile Overall Delivery Time

Definition:
 Time within which 95% of orders are delivered

👉 This is your true SLA metric

2. 95th Percentile FTD Time (First Time Delivery)

Definition:
 Time taken for successful deliveries (excluding retries/failures)

👉 Why 95th percentile?

  • Removes outliers
  • Reflects real customer experience

👉 Good looks like:

  • 95% orders within SLA (15 mins or defined threshold)

B. Time Component Metrics

1. Pick Up Time

  • Measures store readiness + rider assignment

👉 Good looks like:

  • Low waiting time
  • Orders ready before rider arrives

2. Last Mile Time

  • Measures delivery efficiency

👉 Good looks like:

  • Optimised zones
  • Controlled radius

3. Handover Time

  • Measures customer interaction

👉 Good looks like:

  • < 1–2 minutes

4. Return Time

  • Measures rider turnaround

👉 Good looks like:

  • Fast return → higher utilisation

C. Supply Metrics

5. Active Riders (per hour)

Definition:
 Number of riders available every hour

👉 Why it matters:

  • Determines ability to meet demand

👉 Good looks like:

  • Supply matches hourly demand curve
  • No rider shortage in peak

D. Efficiency Metrics

6. UTR (Utilisation per Rider per Hour)

Definition:
 Orders completed per rider per hour

👉 Why it matters:

  • Core efficiency metric
  • Drives cost per order

👉 Good looks like:

  • High UTR without SLA drop

5. How to think about these together

SLA = Time Metrics

  • Pick up
  • Last mile
  • Handover

Capacity = Riders

  • Active riders

Efficiency = UTR

  • Orders per rider

👉 Balance required:

  • Too many riders → low UTR (high cost)
  • Too few riders → SLA breaks

6. What good looks like (overall)

  • 95% delivery within SLA
  • Pick up time minimal
  • Last mile optimised
  • Riders available at all peak hours
  • UTR optimised per store
  • No delivery delays due to supply gaps

7. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Ignoring pick up delays (store issue disguised as logistics issue)
  • Over-hiring riders → low utilisation
  • Under-hiring riders → SLA failure
  • Large delivery radius → high last mile time
  • Not tracking hourly rider supply

8. How this connects to other functions

Operations

  • Impacts pick up time

Instock

  • Impacts order readiness

Growth

  • Drives demand → impacts rider requirement

9. Simple way to think about it

Logistics answers:

👉 “Can we deliver every order fast enough, with the right number of riders?”

10. Key takeaway

Logistics is successful when:

👉 Customers receive orders on time
👉 Riders are fully utilised
👉 Costs are optimised

Fulfilment

FULFILMENT

Fulfilment is the engine of execution.

It ensures:

  • Inventory flows correctly
  • Orders are picked and dispatched accurately
  • Dark stores are replenished on time
  • Customers receive orders within 15 minutes

Fulfilment has two core layers:

  • Operations (End-to-End Flow)
  • Warehouse Readiness (Pre-launch setup)

1. OPERATIONS

Principle

Ensure accurate, fast, and traceable movement of inventory from warehouse → dark stores → customer.

What needs to be done

A. Inbound (Receiving → QC → Putaway)

What happens
  • Inventory comes from vendors or other warehouses
  • Items are:
    • Received
    • Quality checked
    • Put away into correct locations
Key steps
  • ASN receiving with QC pass / fail flow
  • Separate:
    • QC PASS inventory
    • QC FAIL inventory (with reason + images)
  • Create batches for:
    • Different SKUs
    • Different expiry dates
Putaway
  • Scan SKU → assign system location → confirm quantity
  • System enforces:
    • Correct zone placement
    • No zone breach

👉 Ensures:

  • Inventory accuracy
  • Location traceability

B. Inventory Management

Principle

Inventory in system = inventory physically available

What needs to be done
  • Cycle counts / stocktakes regularly
  • Track all movements in WMS
  • Maintain audit trail
Key processes
  • Stock counting and reconciliation
  • Internal stock transfers tracked in system
  • Expiry management (FEFO enforced)

C. Missing Incident Handling

What happens

When picker marks item as missing → incident is created

Two scenarios
  • Actually missing (inventory mismatch)
  • Picker error (item exists but missed)
Resolution flow
  • Scan location
  • Scan SKU
  • Confirm quantity
  • Close job

👉 Ensures:

  • Inventory accuracy
  • Reduced picking errors

D. Outbound (Picking → Sorting → Dispatch)

Principle

Fast, accurate picking = fast delivery

Picking
  • Pick lists generated from orders
  • Follow optimized pick path (serpentine flow)
  • Avoid backtracking

👉 Benefits:

  • Faster picking
  • Reduced congestion
  • Higher accuracy
Monitoring
  • Picking dashboard tracks:
    • Pending quantity
    • Picked quantity
    • Zone-level performance
Sorting & Dispatch
  • Orders sorted store-wise
  • Packed into totes
  • Merged into pallets
  • Dispatched to dark stores

E. Warehouse → Dark Store Transfers

What happens
  • Inventory allocated store-wise
  • Bulk picked → sorted → dispatched
Special case: Near expiry
  • Identify SKUs (30–45 days shelf life)
  • Consolidate → allocate → dispatch
Key rules
  • Label clearly as “NEAR EXPIRY”
  • Separate storage at dark stores
  • Enforce FIFO

F. Returns Flow

  • Items returned from stores
  • Classified into:
    • Restock
    • RTV
    • Disposal

What good looks like

  • Inventory accuracy ≥ 98%
  • No untracked stock movement
  • Picking accuracy high (minimal missing incidents)
  • FEFO followed strictly
  • Warehouse → DS transfers on time
  • Minimal stock damage / expiry loss

Checklist (subtasks)

Inbound

  • ASN receiving live
  • QC pass/fail implemented
  • Putaway system working

Inventory

  • Stocktake process active
  • Movement tracking in WMS
  • Expiry checks in place

Outbound

  • Picking flow tested
  • Pick path optimized
  • Dashboard live

Transfers

  • Store allocation logic defined
  • Dispatch flow tested

Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • Inventory matches system
  • Picking errors minimal
  • End-to-end flow works

FAIL if:

  • Missing incidents high
  • Inventory mismatch
  • Delays in picking / dispatch

2. WAREHOUSE READINESS

Principle

Warehouse must be fully operational, compliant, and scalable before launch

What needs to be done

A. Warehouse Setup

Layout
  • Defined zones:
    • Inbound
    • Storage (ambient / chiller / frozen)
    • Outbound
    • Dispatch
  • Storage vs processing areas clearly separated

B. Storage Infrastructure

  • Racks installed:
    • Ambient
    • Chiller
    • Frozen
  • Bins placed across racks
  • Pallet locations created in system

C. Material Handling Equipment

  • Reach trucks
  • BOPT / HOPT
  • Trolleys
  • Totes
  • All equipment:
    • Tested
    • Operational
    • AMC in place

D. IT & Systems

  • WMS live
  • Warehouse code created
  • PDAs deployed
  • Wi-Fi coverage complete

E. Operational Areas

  • Inbound staging ready
  • Outbound staging ready
  • QC tables installed
  • Sorting areas defined

F. Cold Chain

  • Chiller: 0–4°C
  • Frozen: ≤ -18°C
  • Temperature:
    • Logged
    • Monitored
    • Calibrated

G. Security & Compliance

  • CCTV installed
  • Frisking protocol active
  • Access controlled

H. Floor Marking & Signage

  • Aisles marked
  • Zones labelled
  • Safety signage installed

I. Manpower & Training

  • Headcount planned
  • Teams hired
  • Training completed:
    • WMS
    • Safety
    • SOPs

J. Facility & Admin

  • Cleaning completed
  • Pest control active
  • Pantry & utilities ready

K. Audit & Go-Live

  • Full walkthrough completed
  • WMS tested end-to-end
  • First inbound scheduled

What good looks like

  • Warehouse fully functional before Day 0
  • All systems tested
  • No dependency on post-launch fixes
  • Audit passed

Checklist (subtasks)

Infrastructure

  • Racks installed
  • Bins placed
  • Pallets ready

Systems

  • WMS live
  • PDAs working
  • Wi-Fi stable

Operations

  • Inbound tested
  • Outbound tested
  • Dispatch tested

Compliance

  • Safety checks done
  • Pest control active
  • CCTV live

Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • Warehouse fully operational
  • All flows tested
  • Compliance met

FAIL if:

  • Any core process not working
  • Systems not live
  • Safety/compliance gaps

Final takeaway

Fulfilment is not just a function.

👉 It is the backbone of the 15-minute promise

If this is weak:

  • Speed fails
  • Availability fails
  • Customer trust fails

Warehouse

Warehouse: Real estate, racking & fit-outs

1. What this is responsible for

This function ensures:

👉 A warehouse is identified, built, and made operational
 👉 It can store, process, and dispatch inventory efficiently
 👉 It supports current scale + future expansion

This is a Day 0 critical dependency.

2. Principle

Pick and build warehouses that:

  • Enable fast operations
  • Support correct storage (ambient / chilled / frozen)
  • Allow smooth movement of goods
  • Scale with growing OPD and store count

3. Real estate (warehouse selection)

Principle

Select locations that optimise:

👉 Inbound efficiency
👉 Outbound speed (to dark stores)
👉 Cost

What needs to be done

A. Location selection

Identify warehouse locations based on:

  • Proximity to:
    • Dark stores
    • Demand clusters
  • Accessibility:
    • Truck movement
    • Loading/unloading space
  • Connectivity:
    • Highways
    • Supplier access

B. Site evaluation

Before finalising, check:

  • Total area vs requirement
  • Ceiling height (for racking)
  • Floor load capacity
  • Power availability
  • Water supply
  • Parking / docking bays

C. Commercials & contracts

  • Negotiate:
    • Rent
    • Lock-in
    • Exit clauses
  • Ensure:
    • Fit-out permissions
    • Cold room installation allowed

Output

  • Warehouse location finalised
  • Lease agreement signed
  • Site ready for fit-out

4. Racking (storage design)

Principle

Design storage for:

👉 Maximum utilisation
👉 Easy access
👉 Operational efficiency

What needs to be done

A. Define storage types

Separate zones for:

  • Ambient
  • Chiller (0–4°C)
  • Frozen (≤ -18°C)

B. Rack design

  • Define:
    • Number of bays
    • Levels per bay
    • Bin placement
  • Maintain:
    • Standard dimensions
    • Consistent layout

C. Capacity planning

  • Calculate:
    • Required storage capacity
  • Factor:
    • SKU count
    • Inventory holding days
    • Growth buffer

D. Layout planning

  • Design:
    • Aisles
    • Movement paths
  • Ensure:
    • No congestion
    • Smooth picking

E. System mapping

  • Map racks to:
    • WMS locations
  • Ensure:
    • Each bin is uniquely identifiable

Output

  • Racks installed
  • Storage zones defined
  • System locations mapped

5. Fit-outs (warehouse setup)

Principle

Build a warehouse that is:

👉 Fully functional from Day 1
👉 Safe, compliant, and efficient

What needs to be done

A. Civil & layout works

  • Flooring checked and reinforced
  • Zoning marked:
    • Inbound
    • Storage
    • Outbound
    • Dispatch

B. Cold rooms

  • Install:
    • Chillers
    • Freezers
  • Ensure:
    • Temperature compliance
    • Backup systems

C. Electrical & IT

  • Power supply ready
  • Backup (generator / UPS)
  • Wi-Fi coverage across warehouse
  • WMS devices (PDAs) deployed

D. Material handling equipment

  • Procure:
    • Reach trucks
    • Pallet movers
    • Trolleys
    • Totes
  • Ensure:
    • Fully operational
    • Tested

E. Operational setup

  • Inbound area ready
  • QC stations set up
  • Sorting areas defined
  • Dispatch area ready

F. Safety & compliance

  • CCTV installed
  • Fire safety systems active
  • Signage and floor markings done
  • Pest control active

G. Final readiness

  • End-to-end flow tested:
    • Inbound → Putaway → Picking → Dispatch
  • First inbound planned

Output

  • Warehouse fully operational
  • All systems live
  • Ready for inventory

6. What good looks like

  • Warehouse operational before Day 0
  • Racking fully installed and mapped
  • Cold chain working without failure
  • End-to-end flow tested
  • No dependency on post-launch fixes

👉 Simple test:
 Can inventory be received today and dispatched to stores without issues?

7. Checklist (subtasks)

Real estate

  • Location finalised
  • Lease signed
  • Site handed over

Racking

  • Design completed
  • Racks installed
  • Zones created
  • WMS mapping done

Fit-outs

  • Civil work completed
  • Cold rooms installed
  • IT systems live
  • Equipment ready

Operations readiness

  • Inbound tested
  • Picking tested
  • Dispatch tested

8. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • Warehouse fully functional
  • All flows tested
  • Storage + movement optimised

FAIL if:

  • Racks incomplete
  • Systems not live
  • Cold chain not stable
  • Flow not tested

9. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Underestimating storage requirements
  • Poor layout causing congestion
  • Delayed cold room setup
  • No system mapping
  • Launching without testing flows

Key takeaway

Warehouse setup is not just infrastructure.

👉 It is the foundation of fulfilment and availability

DS & WH Operations

Operations (warehouse → dark store → order fulfilment)

1. What this function is responsible for

Operations is responsible for:

  • Moving inventory from:
    • Vendors → Warehouse → Dark Stores
  • Managing:
    • Transfers
    • Putaway
    • Picking
  • Ensuring:
    • Orders are fulfilled accurately and fast

This function directly impacts:

👉 Fill rate
👉 Picking speed
👉 Delivery SLA
👉 Wastage

2. What good looks like

Flow

  • Inventory moves:
    • Smoothly
    • On time
    • Without delays

Accuracy

  • No:
    • Wrong SKUs
    • Missing items
  • High pick accuracy

Speed

  • Fast:
    • Putaway
    • Picking
  • No bottlenecks

Control

  • Clear visibility of:
    • Stock movement
    • Store-level inventory

👉 Simple test:
 Can inventory move and orders be fulfilled without delays or errors?

3. Core components of operations

A. Warehouse → Dark store transfers

What this is

Movement of inventory from central warehouse to dark stores

What needs to be done

  • Plan transfers based on:
    • Demand (Instock)
    • Store capacity
  • Create:
    • Transfer orders
  • Execute:
    • Dispatch → transit → receiving

What good looks like

  • Timely transfers
  • No delays in replenishment
  • Stores never starved of stock

👉 Failure here = stock-outs at store level

B. Putaway (inventory placement)

What this is

Placing received inventory into correct storage locations

What needs to be done

  • Receive inventory
  • Scan and verify
  • Place into:
    • Correct racks
    • Correct bins

What good looks like

  • Correct SKU placement
  • Easy pick access
  • No misplacement

👉 Failure here = slow picking + wrong orders

C. Picking (order fulfilment)

What this is

Picking items from shelves to fulfil an order

What needs to be done

  • Assign picker
  • Pick items quickly
  • Ensure:
    • Accuracy
    • Completeness

What good looks like

  • Fast picking time
  • High accuracy
  • No missing items

👉 Picking time directly impacts 15-min SLA

D. Store-level inventory management

What this is

Managing inventory inside the dark store

What needs to be done

  • Track:
    • Stock levels
  • Monitor:
    • Fast-moving SKUs
  • Prevent:
    • Stock-outs
    • Overstock

What good looks like

  • High availability
  • Low wastage
  • Clean inventory records

E. Returns & adjustments

What this is

Handling:

  • Damaged items
  • Expired items
  • Inventory mismatches

What needs to be done

  • Identify discrepancies
  • Adjust inventory
  • Track losses

What good looks like

  • Minimal shrinkage
  • Controlled wastage

4. Execution flow (end-to-end)

Step 1: Inbound to warehouse

  • Vendor delivers inventory
  • Inventory received and checked

Step 2: Transfer planning

  • Instock defines:
    • Store requirements
  • Operations creates:
    • Transfer plan

Step 3: Warehouse → store transfer

  • Inventory dispatched
  • Delivered to dark stores

Step 4: Store receiving & putaway

  • Inventory received
  • Verified
  • Stored correctly

Step 5: Order picking

  • Orders come in
  • Items picked
  • Packed for delivery

Step 6: Handover to logistics

  • Orders passed to riders
  • Delivery starts

5. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: Transfers

  • Transfer plan created
  • Inventory dispatched
  • Stores receive stock

Task: Putaway

  • Inventory placed correctly
  • No SKU misplacement

Task: Picking

  • Pickers assigned
  • Orders picked quickly
  • No missing items

Task: Inventory control

  • Stock tracked
  • Adjustments made
  • Wastage controlled

6. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • Transfers on time
  • Picking fast and accurate
  • Inventory accurate
  • No major stock issues

FAIL if:

  • Delayed transfers
  • Picking errors
  • Inventory mismatch
  • High wastage

7. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Poor transfer planning
  • Slow putaway
  • SKU misplacement
  • Ignoring inventory discrepancies
  • Not tracking picking time

8. Simple way to think about it

Operations ensures:

👉 Inventory moves
👉 Orders are picked
👉 Customers get what they ordered

Key takeaway

Operations is where:

👉 Planning becomes reality

Without strong operations:

  • Instock fails
  • Logistics fails
  • Customer experience fails

In-Stock

Instock (availability & supply execution)

1. What this function is responsible for

Instock is responsible for:

  • Ensuring SKUs are available to sell
  • Managing:
    • Demand planning
    • Inventory levels
    • Replenishment
  • Driving:
    • High fill rates
    • Low stock-outs

This function directly impacts:

👉 Conversion
👉 Customer experience
👉 Revenue

2. What good looks like

Availability

  • High fill rates across:
    • SKUs
    • Categories
  • No stock-outs on:
    • KVIs
    • High demand items

Efficiency

  • Right inventory levels:
    • No overstock
    • No understock

Execution

  • Orders fulfilled:
    • On time
    • Without substitutions

👉 Simple test:
 If a customer wants to buy it, is it available?

3. Why instock matters

1. Availability = revenue

  • If SKU is not available:
    • It cannot be sold
  • Lost availability = lost orders

2. Availability drives trust

  • Customers expect:
    • Reliability
  • Repeated stock-outs:
    • Break trust

3. Availability impacts pricing efficiency

  • Promos on unavailable SKUs:
    • Waste burn
  • Pricing without stock:
    • Is meaningless

4. Core metrics

Fill rate

  • % of demand fulfilled

In-stock rate

  • % of SKUs available

Stock-outs

  • Missing SKUs at point of demand

Wastage

  • Expired or unsold inventory

5. How to think about instock

1. Balance is key

Too little stock → stock-outs
Too much stock → wastage

👉 Goal = optimal inventory

2. Not all SKUs are equal

KVIs
  • Must never go out of stock
Core SKUs
  • Maintain consistent availability
Long tail
  • Optimise for efficiency

3. Demand drives supply

  • Plan inventory based on:
    • Demand signals
    • Historical trends
    • Market insights

6. Execution (end-to-end flow)

Step 1: Demand planning

What needs to be done

    • SKU level

  • Use:
    • Market benchmarks

Output

What needs to be done

Step 3: Supply planning

What needs to be done

  • Align:

Output

Step 4: Purchase order (PO) execution

What needs to be done

  • Confirm:
    • Vendor acceptance

Output

Step 5: Inbound & receiving

What needs to be done

  • Validate:

    • Quality
    • Expiry

Output

Step 6: Replenishment

What needs to be done

  • Reorder:

Output

Step 7: Monitoring & correction

What needs to be done

Track:

Take action

9. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Over-ordering without demand
  • Under-ordering KVIs

  • Poor vendor coordination

10. Simple way to think about it

Instock is done when:

👉 The right product
👉 Is available
👉 At the right time

Key takeaway

Commercial builds supply.
Instock makes it sell.

👉 Without instock, everything else breaks:

  • Pricing
  • Promos
  • Customer experience

In-stock - process

Instock (how it actually functions end-to-end)

1. What Instock really does

Instock is not just “keeping items in stock”.

👉 It is a forecast-driven supply system that decides:

  • What to buy
  • How much to buy
  • Where to send it
  • When to replenish

Across:

  • Warehouse
  • Dark stores

2. Core idea (very important)

👉 Instock = Prediction → Planning → Execution

3. End-to-end flow (simple view)

Step 1: Demand forecasting

What happens

System predicts:

👉 Sales for next 7 days
At:

  • SKU level
  • Store level

What it uses

  • Historical sales
  • Day of week patterns
  • Price / promos
  • Availability
  • Trends

Output

👉 “This SKU will sell X units in Store Y”

👉 This is the foundation of everything

Step 2: Reorder point (ROP logic)

What happens

System calculates:

👉 Minimum inventory required per SKU per store

Formula (simplified)

For high demand SKUs:

Reorder Point = Demand + Uncertainty + Lead Time demand

For low demand SKUs:

👉 Heuristics (1–2 units)

Output

👉 “Store needs at least X units to not go out of stock”

👉 This prevents:

  • stock-outs
  • overstock

Step 3: Manual adjustments (critical)

What happens

Instock team overrides system:

  • Supply issues
  • New launches
  • Promotions
  • Market insights

👉 This is called:
Wishlist

Why this matters

Models are good
👉 Humans fix edge cases

Step 4: ATS (Auto Transfer System)

What happens

System decides:

👉 What to transfer
👉 From warehouse → to stores

How it prioritises

  • DRR (daily run rate)
  • Inventory shortage
  • Probability of selling

Key concept

👉 Not all SKUs are treated equally

System prioritises:

  • High probability sales
  • High urgency SKUs

👉 This is extremely powerful

Step 5: Transfer execution

What happens

  • Transfers created
  • Warehouse picks inventory
  • Sent to stores

Constraints

  • Truck capacity
  • Ops capacity
  • Backend stock

Step 6: Store availability

What happens

  • Inventory reaches store
  • Putaway done
  • SKU becomes available

👉 Now:

  • Customer can order

4. Key concepts simplified

1. DRR (Daily Run Rate)

👉 How fast a SKU sells

  • High DRR → critical SKU
  • Low DRR → low priority

2. DOC (Days of Cover)

👉 How many days stock will last

  • Low DOC → urgent transfer
  • High DOC → no action needed

3. Probability-based picking

System asks:

👉 “What is the probability this unit will sell?”

  • High probability → transfer
  • Low probability → skip

4. Guardrails

To prevent:

  • Over-ordering
  • Under-ordering

Examples:

  • Same-day-of-week trends
  • Last 7 days behaviour

5. What good looks like (real instock)

Availability

  • High fill rate
  • No stock-outs on KVIs

Efficiency

  • Low wastage
  • No overstock

System performance

  • Forecast accuracy high
  • Minimal manual correction

Execution

  • Transfers on time
  • Stores always stocked

👉 Simple test:
 Customer wants something → it is available

6. Metrics to track (very important)

Availability

  • Fill rate
  • In-stock %

Supply

  • Lead time
  • Transfer SLA

Efficiency

  • Wastage
  • Overstock

Accuracy

  • Forecast accuracy (MAPE / WAPE)

7. Where instock fails (important)

1. Bad forecast

→ wrong inventory

2. Poor transfer execution

→ stock stuck in warehouse

3. No manual override

→ system blind spots

4. Logistics disconnect

→ stock available but not delivered

8. How it connects to everything

Commercial

  • Defines SKUs
  • Defines supply

Operations

  • Executes transfers
  • Handles putaway

Logistics

  • Needs stock to deliver

Growth

  • Drives demand

👉 Instock sits in the middle of everything

9. Simple way to think about it

Instock answers:

👉 “Will the product be there when the customer orders?”

10. Key takeaway

Instock is not inventory management.

👉 It is a predictive supply engine

  • Forecast demand
  • Calculate need
  • Move stock
  • Keep availability high

Noon in Minutes | Wholesale System

1. Creating a Purchase Order

A Purchase Order (PO) links a vendor to their agreed price list and covers all stock received over the year. It is auto-approved on creation and stays open for 12 months.

How to Create

Tool: https://po.noon.team/9411 → Purchase Order → Create

Select the correct country:

  • 9411 — UAE
  • 9311 — KSA
  • 473914 — Egypt
  • 451559 — Qatar
  • 451558 — Bahrain
FieldWhat to Enter
Order TypeAlways 'Costlist'
Vendor NameSelect the vendor
Price List NameAppears after selecting order type + vendor
Country / CurrencyMatch vendor contract
Item Reference TypeMust be set to 'pbarcode'
Department / Goods Origin / Shipment / Payment TermsAs per vendor contract
Buyer EmailResponsible buyer's email
PO details cannot be edited after saving. Cancel and recreate if anything is wrong.
This PO type auto-approves on creation. No manual approval needed.

Key Differences from a Standard PO

FeatureHow It Works
ApprovalAutomatic on creation
EditingNot allowed — cancel and recreate
Order communicationDone through the Ordering Tool, not a buysheet
Duration12 months, covering multiple orders and dark stores
Goods receipt recordsNot shown in tool — check the data warehouse

2. Pricing & Cost Controls

How Prices Are Pulled

When an order is created, the system finds the agreed price for each product from the vendor price list, using the order date as the reference.

  • Standard price — no end date; stays active until replaced
  • Promotional price — has a start and end date; system reverts to standard price when it expires

Price Change Limits

The system blocks a price change if either of the following limits is exceeded:

LimitValue
Maximum % change50%
Maximum absolute change10 currency units
The restriction applies if either limit is exceeded — it does not need to be both.

If your update is being blocked, contact the Pricing team: tdevavarapu@noon.com, niagrawal@noon.com

Who Can Override Restrictions

TeamWhat They Can Override
Cost Admin teamAll restrictions — date limits, price change limits, approval status
Pricing teamPrice change % and absolute value limits only

Date Restriction on Price Updates

Prices cannot be updated if the start date is more than 1 day in the past. This prevents backdated changes to already-settled accounts.

To override, contact Finance: aknair@noon.com, cagheda@noon.com, hgoyal@noon.com, maralkar@noon.com

Price Variance Warning

The ordering tool should show a warning when a submitted price differs significantly from what is expected.

Confirm with Tech whether this warning is live. If not, get a delivery date and track to closure.

Fixing an Incorrect Price

Situation A — Wrong price in the price list:

  • Re-upload the product with the corrected price (same barcode + same start date). The system will overwrite the old entry.
  • Or set the wrong line to inactive (0) and upload a new correct line.

Situation B — System is blocking the change:

  • Contact the Pricing team to request a temporary override.
  • Once lifted, re-upload the corrected price.

Situation C — Finance needs to make the correction:

For cases where Commercial cannot update directly (e.g. a free item set at 0.01 needing its real price):

Form: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScWFd3dM2wo3hAF0VBu-c2C-PMY3rgHEdkDIw5fEZlFziE-Cg/formResponse

Include: vendor name, product barcode, incorrect price, and correct price. Finance will apply the correction.

3. Replenishment Orders

Tool: https://ro.mx.noon.team/

A replenishment order tells a vendor how many units of each product to send to a specific dark store. Prices are pulled automatically from the vendor price list.

Creating an Order

Click Create Order (top-right). Upload your order sheet — drag and drop or select the file.

ColumnNotes
Vendor CodeMust match the vendor on the linked PO
Warehouse CodeThe dark store receiving the goods
CategoryProduct category
Order DateUsed to look up the correct price — format YYYY-MM-DD
Product BarcodeMust exist in the price list and be set up in the catalogue
QuantityUnits being ordered
If any barcode is missing from the price list or not set up in the catalogue, the entire sheet is rejected. Fix all issues before resubmitting.

Review the system summary before confirming. Click Confirm and Upload to proceed.

Bulk Uploads

One sheet can contain orders for multiple vendors, warehouses, or dates. The system separates them automatically based on unique combinations of vendor, warehouse, category, and order date.

Order Approval

RoleDark Store LimitCentral Warehouse Limit
Standard ApproverNo limitNo limit
Level 1 ApproverUp to AED 20,000Up to AED 100,000
Level 2 ApproverNot allowedUp to AED 400,000
Only one approver is needed per order, as long as they have the right authority for that order value.

Auto-approval: If you have approval authority, orders you upload are approved automatically. The sheet defaults to Approval = On. No extra steps needed.

The system does not notify anyone when an order is held for approval. Always check the order status after uploading.

Manual approval: Go to the Pending Orders tab. Approvers can Approve or Cancel pending orders from there.

Automatic Actions (set on the second tab of the order sheet)

ActionDefaultRequirement
Approve orderOnMust have approval authority
Create delivery recordOffOrder must be approved first
Send to vendorOffOrder must be approved first
Cross-dock deliveryOffTurn on manually if needed

4. Delivery Records & Scheduling

Creating a Delivery Record

Once an order is approved, open the Order Details page and click Create Delivery Record. This is instant — no approval needed. Multiple delivery records can be created against one order for partial deliveries.

ButtonWhat It Does
DocumentsUpload the invoice or supporting paperwork for this delivery
View DetailsSee goods receipt information from the warehouse

Delivery Time Window

Delivery records can only be created up to the 21st of the month following the order creation date.

If an order is too old, the system will block delivery record creation. Contact Tech if this is blocking you.
Cross-dock deliveries can only be scheduled in a morning or evening slot.

Scheduling at the Warehouse

Creating a delivery record does not automatically book a slot at the warehouse. If a time slot is needed, coordinate directly with the warehouse operations team — this is done outside the ordering tool.

Uploading Delivery Documents

Click the Documents button next to a delivery record. Accepted file types: PDF, JPG, JPEG, PNG.

  • Select the document to upload.
  • Preview if it is an image (PDFs cannot be previewed but upload correctly).
  • Confirm. The file is saved with the name you gave it.
  • Deleted files remain visible in the list and cannot be restored through the tool.

Cancelling an Order

An order can be cancelled only if no delivery record exists and it has not been sent to the vendor.

Once a delivery record is created or the order has been sent to the vendor, it cannot be cancelled.

Updating an Export After Price Changes

  • Open the Order Details page and click Clear Export.
  • The order goes back to Waiting for Approval — re-approve it.
  • Download the updated export and resend to the vendor.

OPD Targets

OPD (orders per day planning)

1. What OPD is

OPD (Orders Per Day) is the target number of orders the business aims to achieve on a daily basis.

It is the primary driver of scale and directly impacts:

  • Revenue
  • Utilisation (riders, stores)
  • Cost efficiency
  • Profitability

2. Why OPD matters

1. It aligns all functions

OPD is not owned by one team.

It is built jointly by:

  • Growth → drives demand
  • Commercial → ensures assortment & pricing
  • Logistics → ensures delivery capacity
  • On-site (app) → ensures conversion

👉 Without a clear OPD target, teams operate in silos

2. It defines capacity planning

OPD determines:

  • Number of riders required
  • Inventory levels
  • Dark store utilisation

3. It drives profitability

  • Higher OPD →
    • Better fixed cost absorption
    • Better utilisation

👉 But only if:

  • Costs are controlled (PC1)

3. Link to AOP (non-negotiable)

OPD targets must come from AOP

  • OPD is not estimated arbitrarily
  • It is derived from:
    • AOP growth plan
    • Revenue targets

👉 Similarly:

  • PC1 targets must also align with AOP

What this means

  • Growth cannot:
    • Chase OPD at any cost
  • Commercial & pricing must:
    • Protect PC1

👉 Balance required:

  • OPD (scale)
  • PC1 (profitability)

4. When OPD must be defined

OPD must be closed at least 1 week before launch

Why this is critical

OPD drives:

  • Marketing spend planning
  • Rider hiring
  • Inventory planning
  • Store readiness

👉 Without OPD:

  • No function can plan correctly

5. How OPD is built

Step 1: Start with AOP

  • Monthly OPD target derived from:
    • AOP plan

Step 2: Break into channels

Growth defines contribution from:

  • Core (existing traffic)
  • Performance marketing
  • Partnerships
  • Affiliates
  • Organic

Step 3: Align with operations

Validate with:

  • Logistics:
    • Can riders handle demand?
  • Instock:
    • Is inventory sufficient?
  • Commercial:
    • Is assortment ready?

Step 4: Define ramp-up plan

  • OPD does not start at peak

Define:

  • Day 1 OPD
  • Week 1 OPD
  • Month-end OPD

Step 5: Define backup plan

  • If OPD is not achieved:
    • Additional campaigns
    • Partnerships
    • Offers

6. What good looks like

  • OPD target:
    • Clearly defined
    • Closed before launch
  • Channel contribution:
    • Clearly mapped
  • Ramp-up plan:
    • Defined
  • Alignment:
    • Across all functions

👉 Simple test:
 Can every team answer:

  • What OPD is expected?
  • How it will be achieved?

7. Checklist (subtasks)

Task: OPD planning

  • OPD derived from AOP
  • PC1 targets aligned
  • Channel split defined

Task: Cross-functional alignment

  • Logistics capacity validated
  • Inventory aligned
  • Assortment ready

Task: Execution readiness

  • Marketing plan aligned
  • Ramp-up plan defined
  • Backup plan ready

8. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • OPD defined before launch
  • PC1 aligned with AOP
  • All functions aligned

FAIL if:

  • No clear OPD target
  • Misalignment across teams
  • Unrealistic targets
  • No ramp-up plan

9. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Setting OPD without AOP
  • Ignoring PC1 while chasing growth
  • Not aligning logistics capacity
  • No backup plan
  • Late planning

10. Simple way to think about it

OPD answers:

👉 “How many orders should the business deliver daily?”

Key takeaway

OPD is not just a target.

👉 It is the anchor that aligns growth, operations, and profitability

Procurement

1. What this function is responsible for

Procurement ensures:

  • All required materials, services, and assets are sourced
  • Vendors are selected based on speed, cost, and reliability
  • Spend is controlled and aligned with CAPEX and OPEX targets

This function directly impacts:

👉 Store launch timelines
👉 Cost efficiency
👉 Quality of infrastructure (fit-outs, equipment, etc.)

2. Core idea

Procurement is about:

👉 Getting the right vendor, at the right cost, at the right time

Not just cheapest — but balanced across speed + price + reliability

3. Vendor classification

All vendors are classified into 3 levels:

Level 1: Fastest / Premium Vendors

  • Highest cost
  • Fastest turnaround
  • Most reliable

👉 Used when timelines are critical or launch is at risk.

Level 2: Balanced Vendors

  • Moderate cost
  • Reasonable speed
  • Reliable

👉 Default choice for most requirements.

Level 3: Cost-Optimised Vendors

  • Lowest cost
  • Slower execution
  • Variable reliability

👉 Used when timelines are flexible and cost saving is the priority.

This classification ensures clear decision-making and no delays due to vendor confusion.

4. Procurement process

Step 1: Requirement definition

  • Identify what needs to be procured
  • Define specifications and timelines

Step 2: RFQ creation (via Procol)

  • Raise RFQ (Request for Quotation) on Procol
  • Invite multiple vendors

Step 3: Vendor comparison

Compare vendors on: Price, Delivery timelines, Quality, Past performance.

Step 4: Vendor selection

  • Choose vendor based on priority (speed vs cost)
  • Assign vendor level (L1 / L2 / L3)

Step 5: Finalisation

  • Confirm scope, pricing, and timelines
  • Proceed with contracting (via Legal / SpotDraft if required)

Step 6: Execution tracking

  • Monitor delivery timelines, quality, and completion status

5. What good looks like

  • Multiple vendor options for each requirement
  • Clear vendor comparison (not single sourcing)
  • Procurement aligned with timelines
  • No delays due to vendor issues
  • Costs within defined budgets

6. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Selecting vendors without comparison
  • Prioritising only cost (ignoring speed)
  • Delayed RFQ creation
  • Poor specification leading to wrong vendor output
  • Not tracking vendor performance

7. How it connects to other functions

  • Real Estate / Dark Stores — Fit-outs, racking, cold rooms
  • IT — Devices, internet setup
  • Operations — Equipment, store setup
  • Finance — Budget control, payments

8. Simple way to think about it

Procurement answers: 👉 "Who will do this work, how fast, and at what cost?"

Key takeaway

Procurement is a decision engine: speed vs cost trade-offs, vendor selection clarity, and execution reliability.

Done well: 👉 Launches are fast and cost-efficient
Done poorly: 👉 Delays + cost overruns

9. Tools

Procol

Used for raising RFQs, comparing vendors, and standardising procurement. Ensures transparency, better vendor selection, and faster decision-making.

IT Assets & Internet Setup

1. What this function is responsible for

IT ensures that every dark store and ops node has:

  • The hardware required to run operations
  • A stable internet connection at all times
  • All systems (WMS, app, dashboards) working seamlessly

This function directly impacts:

👉 Order processing
👉 Picking speed
👉 Rider coordination
👉 System uptime

2. Core idea

IT is the backbone of operations.

If systems fail: orders stop, picking stops, deliveries get delayed.

3. Key components

A. IT Assets (Hardware Setup)

What this includes:

  • Billing / order processing devices
  • Picking devices (phones / handheld scanners)
  • Label printers
  • Desktop / laptops (store + admin use)
  • Routers / networking equipment

What needs to be done:

  • Procure all required hardware
  • Configure devices with required apps and login credentials
  • Assign devices to store staff and functions

What good looks like:

  • All devices functional before go-live
  • No dependency on personal devices
  • Staff trained on device usage

B. Internet Setup (Connectivity)

What this includes:

  • Primary internet line
  • Backup internet (recommended)
  • Router configuration

What needs to be done:

  • Install internet at all locations: dark stores, warehouse, office (if applicable)
  • Ensure high speed and stable connection
  • Set up backup connection (dongle / secondary ISP)

What good looks like:

  • Zero downtime during operations
  • Fast system response
  • Backup kicks in automatically if primary fails

C. System Access & Configuration

What this includes:

  • WMS / order management system
  • Rider apps
  • Admin dashboards
  • Pricing / commercial tools

What needs to be done:

  • Create user logins for store staff, managers, and central teams
  • Assign correct permissions
  • Test all workflows: order creation, picking, dispatch

What good looks like:

  • All users can log in without issues
  • No permission gaps
  • End-to-end flows tested successfully

4. Pre-launch checklist

IT Assets

  • Devices procured
  • Devices configured
  • Devices assigned

Internet

  • Primary connection live
  • Backup connection ready

Systems

  • All logins created
  • Permissions assigned
  • End-to-end testing completed

5. Audit (pass / fail)

PASS if:

  • All systems working without issues
  • No internet downtime
  • Orders can be processed end-to-end

FAIL if:

  • Devices missing or not configured
  • Internet unstable
  • System access issues
  • Any step in order flow breaks

6. Common mistakes to avoid

  • Relying on a single internet connection
  • Not testing systems before launch
  • Delayed device procurement
  • Incorrect access/permissions
  • Using personal devices for operations

7. How it connects to other functions

  • Operations — Uses devices for picking and putaway
  • Logistics — Rider apps depend on connectivity
  • Growth / On-site — App experience depends on backend uptime

8. Simple way to think about it

IT ensures: 👉 The system runs   👉 The store functions   👉 Orders move without interruption

Key takeaway

IT is not a support function. 👉 It is mission critical for launch readiness

If IT fails: Operations fail. Logistics fail. Customer experience fails.

1.0 · HOW WE WORK

The house rules.

03 / 11
01

02

If you see it, you own it — or you hand it off on purpose.
03
We measure everything.
If it isn't in a dashboard, it didn't happen.
04
We fix problems immediately.
Small fires put out today. Never inherited by next week.
05
We don't tolerate mediocrity.
The standard is the standard. Kindly, consistently, non-negotiably.
2.1 · OPERATING PRINCIPLES

Five principles. Every. Single. Day.

04 / 11
01 · DEFAULT
Ownership is default.
"That's not my job" is not a sentence in this building.
02 · PACE
Speed over perfection.
Decide fast. Correct fast. Shipped beats polished.
03 · EVIDENCE
We argue with data.
Dashboards > stories. Bring a number or bring a question.
04 · STANDARDS
Standards are binary.
You hit the target or you don't. There is no partial credit.
05 · CADENCE
We improve every day.
1% a day, compounded. That's the whole game.

3.1 · NON-NEGOTIABLES
06 / 11

The four non-negotiables.

No exceptions. No context that changes these.

Customer obsession.
01 /
The customer is the final judge. Not your boss. Not your deck. Not your opinion.
Know your numbers.
02 /
If you run it, you know its numbers cold — in currency, in minutes, in percentage points.
Standards are always high.
03 /
We do not lower the bar for convenience, tenure, or mood.
Zero-BS policy.
04 /
Be transparent. Surface bad news faster than good news. Always.
3.2 · THE LINE
07 / 11

Things we will not tolerate.

Not dramatic. Just firm. The line is visible so nobody trips over it.

  • ✕
    Missed numbers, unexplained.
  • ✕
    Finger-pointing instead of fixing.
  • ✕
    Problems buried. Surprises at review.
  • ✕
    Opinions without numbers.
  • ✕
    Stores out of standard. Again.
  • ✕
    "It's fine" when it isn't.
